lessons.title: Beyond Money Supply: Defining the Global Liquidity Cycle

body.text: Global liquidity is not how much money exists in the world. It is how easily that money can move into risk assets, across borders, and eventually into your portfolio, and that ease expands and contracts in cycles that the Fed, ECB, BOJ and PBOC collectively drive.

children.text: If you check the Nifty on your phone or watch financial news, you have heard "liquidity" used loosely: "there is a lot of liquidity in the market" when FIIs are buying, or "liquidity has dried up" when FPIs are selling. That casual usage is fine for headlines, but it is the wrong starting point for serious analysis. Trading or allocating on the wrong proxy for liquidity is a common and expensive mistake, and it starts with a definition that is too narrow.

body.text: Why money supply alone is the wrong starting point: US M2 grew steadily for decades without producing dramatic swings in asset prices, then grew by roughly a quarter in a single year during 2020. Money supply is a stock. It tells you how much money exists at a point in time, but not how freely that money is moving into risk assets, or whether it is about to reverse. Global liquidity is best understood as a flow, not a stock.

children.text: The Three Layers of Global Liquidity

reserves held by commercial banks at the central bank, plus currency in circulation. This is what shows up directly on a central bank's balance sheet, and it expands when the Fed, ECB, BOJ or PBOC runs quantitative easing.

the lending and borrowing that banks and shadow banks build on top of base money. A unit of central bank reserves can support many units of loans, corporate bonds and repo activity, and this multiplier itself expands and contracts with risk appetite.

the layer that actually connects Fed policy to the Nifty. It includes FPI and FDI flows, the eurodollar market, and cross-currency basis swaps. This is the mechanism by which liquidity created in Washington or Tokyo ends up buying or selling shares on the NSE and BSE.

children.text: Liquidity does not simply grow forever. It moves in cycles: an expansion phase (quantitative easing, rate cuts, active central bank swap lines) followed by a contraction phase (quantitative tightening, rate hikes, swap lines going quiet). These cycles do not line up neatly with GDP growth cycles. An economy can be growing while global liquidity is tightening, and vice versa, which is exactly why the global liquidity cycle deserves its own framework rather than being folded into ordinary business cycle analysis.

body.caption: Two Phases of the Global Liquidity Cycle

cells: Mixed, often supported by low real rates
Pressured by high real rates and a strong dollar

children.text: This matters for Indian investors because the RBI's own tools (the repo rate, CRR, SLR and open market operations) set domestic monetary conditions, but they cannot fully insulate India from the global liquidity cycle. FPI positioning in NSE and BSE-listed stocks and in government securities responds heavily to global dollar liquidity, often more than to domestic RBI policy alone. The rest of this course builds outward from here: Chapter 2 opens up the Fed's own balance sheet mechanics, Chapter 3 places the RBI within the wider pattern of central bank coordination and divergence, and Chapter 4 looks at how equities, gold and crypto each respond differently as liquidity expands and contracts.

body.title: The March 2020 Puzzle
body.scenario: In March 2020, the Fed cut its policy rate to near zero and launched open-ended quantitative easing within weeks. In the same month, FPIs pulled money out of Indian equities at a then-record pace, and the rupee weakened sharply.
body.prompt: If the Fed was flooding the world with liquidity, why did India experience what looked like a liquidity squeeze rather than a flood? What does this tell you about a simple "more central bank money means more liquidity everywhere" model?
body.modelAnswer: The initial COVID shock triggered a dash for cash: a scramble for dollar liquidity as investors sold assets everywhere, including in emerging markets, to raise dollars and de-risk. Even though the Fed was easing, the transmission of that liquidity into global markets takes time to work through swap lines, bank balance sheets and risk appetite. So the sequence was squeeze first, flood later. By the second half of 2020, as the Fed's QE and dollar swap lines with other central banks did their work, FPI flows into India reversed strongly and record inflows followed. The direction of central bank policy and the timing of its market effect are two different things, and mixing them up is one of the more common mistakes in reading the liquidity cycle.

body.title: Check Your Definition
body.question: Which of these is the best definition of the "global liquidity cycle"?
options: The total money supply (M2) of the world's major economies
The expansion and contraction of money and credit creation by major central banks, and its transmission across borders into markets
The RBI's repo rate cycle on its own
The combined market capitalization of global equity markets
body.explanation: Money supply alone is a stock, not a flow, and it says nothing about credit creation or cross-border transmission. The global liquidity cycle is about how much money and credit is being created, and how freely it moves across countries and into risk assets.

points: Global liquidity has three layers: base or core liquidity created directly by central banks, credit liquidity multiplied through the banking system, and cross-border liquidity that transmits it across countries.
Money supply (M2) alone is a weak proxy for liquidity conditions. It does not capture direction, credit creation, or cross-border transmission.
Liquidity moves in cycles of expansion and contraction that do not always match GDP growth cycles.
RBI's domestic tools can cushion but not fully insulate India from the global liquidity cycle, because FPI flows into NSE and BSE respond heavily to global dollar liquidity conditions.
The 2020 COVID shock shows that a liquidity crisis can look like a squeeze even during aggressive central bank easing, because of transmission lags and a scramble for dollar funding.
